item.title: Why a Better AI Teammate Can Mean Lower Team Output
item.description:
Background

Replacing a team member with AI that can do more work seems likely to increase the team’s output. At the very least, if AI does as much work as the person it replaces, we might expect total output to stay the same.

This paper examines theoretically how replacing a human with AI that contributes more can nevertheless reduce team output.

item.title: How Performance Evaluation Shapes Peer Learning Within Teams
item.description:
Background

Organizations rely heavily on employees learning from one another. New-hire training, on-the-job learning, mentoring, and pair work all create opportunities for knowledge to flow from more experienced or skilled workers to their coworkers.

But this learning does not happen automatically. Teaching takes time away from one’s own work. More subtly, teaching can narrow the performance gap between the person who teaches and the person who learns.

item.title: Do Teams That Care About Each Other Perform Worse?
item.description:
Background

Organizations do more than place employees in teams. They invest in shared goals, cohesion, and collective incentives, all intended to make members care about one another’s outcomes. There is good reason to do so: members who care about their teammates seem likely to work hard for the team, and existing work finds that social relationships among coworkers affect workplace effort and that team incentives are more effective in more cohesive teams.

But many of the activities assigned to teams require more than diligent execution. Work is not only a matter of how much members work; it is also a matter of what they work on.
